Every morning at a quarter past six, Meera unlocks the small clinic on Station Road and switches on the old radio by the window.
The first patient is usually Mr. Desai, who is seventy-two, walks with a carved wooden stick, and insists that his blood pressure is perfectly fine.
It never is, of course, but he likes to argue about it while she wraps the cuff around his arm and counts quietly under her breath.
By eight o'clock the waiting room is full: a carpenter with a bandaged thumb, two schoolgirls with fevers, and a young father holding twins who refuse to stop crying.
Meera keeps a notebook with everyone's names, their medicines, and the dates of their next visits, because the computer crashes whenever it rains.
Last Thursday the power went out for almost three hours, and the doctor had to write fourteen prescriptions by hand, squinting under a torch.
Nobody complained. The carpenter fixed the broken hinge on the cupboard, the twins finally fell asleep, and Mr. Desai brought everyone a box of sweets from the market.
Around noon the rush slows down, and Meera eats her lunch of rice, dal, and pickled mango while reading the newspaper backwards, starting with the crossword.
In the afternoon she phones patients who missed their appointments, reminds them gently, and books new slots for Monday, Wednesday, or Friday.
Some people answer on the first ring; others call back late at night, apologising, asking whether the doctor can still see them tomorrow.
She always says yes, even when the diary is already full, because she knows how far some of them travel just to get here.
When the clinic finally closes at seven, she counts the cash twice, waters the plants on the balcony, and switches off the radio, which has been playing the same song all day.
